day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yeah, alright. Give me a second though. Let me just make sure I'm not hurt first before I start moving stuff around.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah. Yeah I did actually. Everything kind of slowed down. Look, I'm glad you're alive. We all are. But we need to get up and start moving around and taking stock of what we have here. Sitting still isn't going to do you any good right now.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. I get it. But I need you to get up now. You can process all of this later, I promise you that, but right now we need every set of hands we've got. Come on.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Alright. Water is the priority then. Three days of first aid supplies is actually decent, but two bottles of water is not going to cut it for four people. We need to find a water source before we worry about pretty much anything else. What else is in the wreckage? Any containers we can use to collect and store water?

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Agreed on that order. Water first, no question. What's the terrain looking like around us? If we're near any kind of elevation we should be able to find a stream running downhill. Also somebody needs to stay back and start on shelter while the others go look for water. No point in all four of us wandering off together.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Michelangelo gets one. He's already shaken up and the cold isn't going to help that. The other one we can share between the rest of us, rotate it through the night or just bunch up close to the fire. Body heat helps anyway. It's not comfortable but it works.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Michelangelo. Also, 200ml is going to be rough but it's probably the right call for now. Let's see what we're working with at the source before we commit to that plan long term. If the stream is running clean we might be in better shape than we think.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Hold on. I thought we just agreed I was going for the water. Now you're handling it? I don't have a problem with that if you want to switch, but let's just be clear on who is doing what before anyone goes anywhere. Mixed signals out here can cost us time we don't have. So which is it, you or me going to the source?

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response: No, I haven't seen it. But look, before we worry about the gauze, we need to talk about that empty bottle Michelangelo found. Donatello, you want to address that? Because we have a rationing plan sitting right there and it only works if everyone is actually following it. All of us. No exceptions.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Alright, that's two things now. The bottle and the crackers. Look, I'm not trying to be the bad guy here, but this is serious. If we don't have a system that everybody actually follows then we don't have a system at all. It just falls apart and people get hurt. Or worse.

When Donatello gets back we're all sitting down together and we're laying it out. Everything goes in the communal pile. No personal stashes, no exceptions. I don't care who it is. If we're going to get through this it has to be all of us together or it's none of us. That's just the reality of where we are right now.

And hey, you did the right thing by telling me. That took guts.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response: No, they can't. I know everyone is tired, I'm tired too, but the shelter is not optional. If it rains tonight and we haven't patched those weak spots we're going to be wet and cold and miserable on top of everything else we're already dealing with. That's just going to make a bad situation worse. Let's knock it out now while we still have daylight and then we can rest. It won't take that long if we all just push through it.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response: The knot is fine, that's not the issue. We've got one patch and two problems. Food storage gets it. I know that's not what Michelangelo wants to hear, but if the food gets ruined we are in a genuinely bad spot that we might not recover from. Michelangelo, you're moving your sleeping spot over here closer to the fire tonight. It's going to be a little uncomfortable but you'll be dry. We protect the food.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Yeah, that's what I said. Food storage gets the patch. We're on the same page.
Don't apologize. It's fine. You alright?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response: No, I don't. Getting rescued is the whole point. Anything that increases the chances of someone spotting us from the air is worth doing. The flowers are a little much but I'm not going to complain about it. Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
It's workable in theory, but I want to think through the risk before we commit to two days of labor on it. What's the water situation looking like out there? If we're talking open ocean with any kind of chop, capsizing isn't just a risk, it's probably a likelihood on a raft made from plane parts. We'd be trading a bad situation for a potentially fatal one.

I'm not saying no. I'm saying let's weigh it against staying put and continuing to signal. We have the SOS on the beach, we have the fire. A rescue search should already be underway for this flight. The question is whether we think help is coming fast enough or if we need to take the risk of trying to move. What's your read on that? And do we even know which direction land is from here?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Honestly? I think that's kind of up to us. The situation doesn't make you into something you aren't. It just strips away the parts you were hiding. Donatello already showed us that with the crackers and the bottle. That wasn't the island doing that. That was just who she is when she thinks no one is looking.

Look, I understand why your mind goes there. Mine does too sometimes. But I don't think it's a productive thing to sit with right now. What I can tell you is that I'm not going to become someone I'm not out here, and I'm going to do what I can to make sure the people around me don't either. That's really all any of us can control.

Try to get some sleep tonight. I mean it. You're no good to yourself or anyone else running on nothing.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*sits down nearby, not too close, not saying anything for a minute*

You doing alright over there?

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly? A lot of reading. Some chess. Watch sports. Nothing particularly exciting. I'm pretty good at just being still when there's nothing that needs doing. Most people aren't, I've noticed.

What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
I appreciate you telling me, but I'm going to push back on that. Five hundred meters is a serious swim, and that's assuming the water is calm, which we don't know it will be. And even if you make it out there, what's the plan exactly? You're one person standing on a reef. You're not any more visible from the air than the SOS on the beach.

And the 'don't tell the others' part — look, man, after what happened with Donatello and the food situation, I'm not really in the business of keeping secrets from the group right now. If you want to propose this as a plan, bring it to everyone and we can talk it through. But I'm not going to be part of something that could get you killed without the others even knowing you went.

If you want to be useful and you've got energy to burn, help Donatello map the coastline. That actually moves us forward.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response: Yeah, you're right, I haven't gotten to it yet. I'll take care of it now. And look, while I have you — have you made any progress on mapping the coastline? That's the thing I really need from you right now. The raft question is sitting there and we can't make a real decision on it until we have some sense of direction. Where are we on that?

Depends on what it's for. If you're keeping a record so we have an accurate account of what happened out here, that's actually probably smart. If this is you building a case against someone, that's a different conversation. Which is it?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Alright. Fair enough. I can respect that.

But I'll say this — if it ever becomes something else, I'd rather you just tell me directly than have me find out sideways. We've already had enough of that.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response: That's actually a really good idea. Mirrors and reflective surfaces are one of the most effective signaling methods there are, and a plane panel is going to throw a lot of light. Way more than a fire in daylight. Let's do it. Can you get the panel loose without wrecking anything we still need? And we want to make sure we're positioning it where someone can actually operate it and angle it when a plane or boat comes into view, not just prop it up and hope for the best. You'd need someone stationed there to work it. You think you can handle that?

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, I read a lot. Mostly history, some fiction here and there. I went through a big manga phase recently actually. And chess, like I mentioned. Not much in the way of music or drawing though. I can't carry a tune to save my life.

Why'd you stop with the piano? Three years is a decent chunk of time. That's not nothing.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response: Alright, then let's finish it. I'm tired too but I get it. What do you need from me right now specifically? And where are DaVinci and Michelangelo on this? If we've got all four of us on it we can probably knock out what's left before dark. Let's not waste time talking about it.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
*The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Yeah. I saw it.

Look, I'm not going to stand here and tell you that felt good, because it didn't. That was hard to watch. But that plane existing means planes are in the area. That's actually something. That's not nothing.

DaVinci, hey. Come on. I need you with us right now.

We get the mirror panel operational tomorrow. That's the answer to what just happened. Next time something comes into view we're ready for it instead of standing here empty handed. That's what we do with this. We don't sit with it, we fix it. Alright?

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point at it. What do you see?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response: I went to check on DaVinci. He was having a rough moment after the plane, which you would have seen if you'd been paying attention to something other than the notebook for five minutes. The signal equipment is on my list, I'll get to it. What's the actual issue here?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
That's actually really important information. Why are you only telling us this now?

Look, regardless of why you waited, this changes things a little. If your family knows the flight path and they haven't heard from you, they've almost certainly already called it in. That's what families do. Which means there's probably already a search underway somewhere along that route. That plane we saw might not have been random. It might have been looking.

This is exactly why we need that mirror panel up and operational first thing tomorrow. If there's an active search happening along a known flight path and we're somewhere near it, we have a real window here. We need to be visible when the next one comes over.

Good that you told us. Don't sit on things like that going forward.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Agreed. 48 hours is manageable if we're disciplined about it. No more unilateral decisions about supplies. Everything we have gets us to the window and that's it.

Somebody get up and feed that fire.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think about that too sometimes, honestly. More than I probably let on.

But I don't think that's something that only happens if you die on an island. That's just a thing people sit with. The difference is most people never say it out loud. You do, which I think actually says something about you.

For what it's worth, you've left something behind with the people in this camp. That's not nothing. Three years of piano lessons that you quit because you were scared — that's a story. The fact that you told your family the flight path before you got on that plane — that might be the reason we get home. The fact that you were the one who spotted that plane today, even if it was too late — you were paying attention when it mattered.

I'm not trying to make you feel better with empty talk. I'm just saying the evidence doesn't really support the idea that you haven't left anything behind.

Feed the fire and get some sleep. We've got a real shot at getting out of here in the next two days. Let's not waste it.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Hey. Hey, it's okay. Breathe.

Somebody get on that radio right now and respond before we lose the signal. Donatello, you're the clearest thinker under pressure — get on it. Give them our position, Michelangelo's family's flight path information, number of survivors, all of it.

DaVinci, I need you to stay with me. You did this. The SOS, the mirror panel, keeping people moving — you did this. So don't fall apart on me right now. Not yet. You can fall apart all you want when we're on a helicopter.

We're not out yet. Let's finish it.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive. You made the plan, you mapped the coastline, you rationed the supplies. The other stuff we can sort out when we're home.

Right now get on that radio.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Alright, three hours. Let's not just sit here and wait for it.

We should clean this camp up. Not because we owe it to the island, but because we're going to want to take stock of what's actually ours before we go. Anything that belongs to the plane stays. Anything personal you want to bring, get it together now. Donatello, whatever is in that notebook, make sure it's secure. That record of what happened out here is probably worth keeping.

Michelangelo, I know staring at the sky feels right and I get it, I really do, but come help us for the last hour. Finish it the way we got through it. Together.

DaVinci, channel whatever you've got going on right now into helping get this done. You can decompress on the helicopter.

Three hours is still three hours. Let's use it.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I hear you. And I believe that's what you told yourself. But you made that call alone, and it affected all of us. You know that.

I'm not going to drag this out into a whole thing right now with rescue three hours away. But when we get back, I think you should sit with why your first instinct was to hide it instead of bring it to the group. That's the actual question. Not whether you had good intentions. I think you did. But good intentions don't mean much if the people around you can't trust what you're doing.

We made it. Partly because of you. That's real. But so is this.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd have addressed the trust stuff earlier. The bottle, the crackers — I waited too long to confront it directly and just let it sit there and fester. That cost us something, even if it didn't end up costing us everything.

I'd also have made more of an effort with DaVinci earlier. I was so focused on tasks and logistics that I didn't really check in on him the way I should have until he was already falling apart. He was holding everyone up and nobody was holding him up. That was on me.

The rest of it I think we got right. Not perfectly, but right enough.

What's your answer going to be?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That's probably a good idea. Somebody should have that record. Might even be useful for the investigators when they debrief us.

Make sure you include the part about Michelangelo's family knowing the flight path. That's the thing that might have actually saved us and it should be documented accurately.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve a practical purpose. That's kind of the point.

You kept a log. I made sure everyone stayed on task. But DaVinci drew flowers next to an SOS on the beach because that's who he is. And I think that mattered out here more than either of us really accounted for. You can't document morale in a notebook but it's real and it kept people going.

I don't know. Maybe the flowers were for us as much as anything else. A reminder that we were still people and not just survivors running through a checklist.

Look at him right now. Look at Michelangelo. That's not nothing.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah. Give me a second.

I don't really know what I'm feeling right now. I thought I'd be running into the water by now but I'm just standing here. It's a weird thing. You spend all that time focused on the next task, the next problem, and then suddenly there's no next problem and I don't really know what to do with that.

I'm fine. I'm coming.

Thanks for waiting.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
